note: Rhode Island's reporting law names this industry directly: under RIGL 40-11-3 every person in the state must report suspected child abuse or neglect within 24 hours, and the law defines abuse to include injury, sexual abuse or exploitation, negligent treatment or maltreatment by any employee of a residential facility or any staff person providing out-of-home care. The same department licenses those facilities and takes the reports.

civil_injury.summary: Three years for injuries to the person, which covers assault, battery and negligence.
civil_injury.quote: Actions for injuries to the person shall be commenced and sued within three (3) years next after the cause of action shall accrue, and not after
civil_injury.note: Rhode Island has no separate, shorter statute for assault, battery or false imprisonment in 9-1-14; they are treated as injuries to the person. Whether false imprisonment without physical injury falls under 9-1-14(b) or the ten-year catch-all (9-1-13) was not confirmed.

civil_minor_tolling.summary: If you were under 18 when you were hurt, the three years start at 18, so the deadline is your 21st birthday.
civil_minor_tolling.quote: If any person at the time any such cause of action shall accrue to him or her shall be under the age of eighteen (18) years, or of unsound mind, or beyond the limits of the United States, the person may bring the cause of action, within the time limited under this chapter, after the impediment ...
civil_minor_tolling.note: No cap. No general discovery rule or extended period for non-sexual child abuse was found; 9-1-51 covers childhood sexual abuse only.

civil_government_claims.summary: Tort claims against the state, a city or town must be filed within three years of the injury; for a city or town, the claim must first be presented to the town or city council.
civil_government_claims.quote: in cases involving actions or claims in tort against the state or any political subdivision thereof or any city or town, the action shall be instituted ... within three (3) years of the accrual of any claim of tort. Failure to institute suit within the three-year (3) period shall constitute a bar
civil_government_claims.note: 45-15-5 (https://webserver.rilegislature.gov/Statutes/TITLE45/45-15/45-15-5.htm) requires presenting the claim to the town or city council and waiting 40 days before suing; it sets no separate deadline. Whether 9-1-19 minority tolling applies to 9-1-25 claims was not confirmed.

criminal_child_abuse.summary: Three years. Rhode Island's felony child abuse law (Brendan's Law) has no special deadline, so the general three-year rule applies, with no pause until the child turns 18.
criminal_child_abuse.quote: The statute of limitations for any other criminal offense shall be three (3) years, unless a longer statute of limitations is otherwise provided for in the general laws.
criminal_child_abuse.note: 11-9-5.3 (https://webserver.rilegislature.gov/Statutes/TITLE11/11-9/11-9-5.3.htm) expressly covers a person having care of a child 'including any instance where a child has been placed by his or her parents, caretaker, or licensed or governmental child placement agency for care or treatment', which fits residential programs. Its maximum penalty is 20 years (40 for a repeat offense), not life, so it is not in the no-limit list in 12-12-17(a). No tolling for minority was found in 12-12-17. Medium only because no search was made for a longer period elsewhere in the general laws.

criminal_felony_assault.summary: Three years for felony assault, and three years for misdemeanor assault as well.
criminal_felony_assault.quote: The statute of limitations for any other criminal offense shall be three (3) years, unless a longer statute of limitations is otherwise provided for in the general laws.
criminal_felony_assault.note: No limit applies to offenses punishable by life imprisonment and to listed crimes such as homicide, robbery and first-degree sexual assault (12-12-17(a)). Felony assault under 11-5-2 carries up to 20 years, so it uses the three-year default.

channels.name: Rhode Island Department of Health, licensee complaints
channels.what_it_can_do: Licenses and disciplines Rhode Island's clinical mental health counselors, marriage and family therapists, social workers and psychologists through its boards, and takes complaints against all of them through one route.
channels.who_to_report: A licensed mental health professional in Rhode Island.
channels.how: Submit a complaint through the Department's licensee complaints page.
channels.phone_note: Psychology Licensing Board. Department main line 401-222-5500.

channels.name: Rhode Island DCYF Licensing
channels.what_it_can_do: Under RI General Law 42-72.1 the Department of Children, Youth and Families licenses, monitors and enforces the regulations for every foster home, residential facility and child-placing agency in the state.
channels.how: Complain to the Department's licensing staff. If you are not satisfied with the decision, there is a right of appeal to a judicial forum.

channels.name: Rhode Island Child Abuse Hotline
channels.what_it_can_do: The statutory report line, open around the clock. Rhode Island law defines reportable abuse to include maltreatment by any employee of a residential facility or staff person providing out-of-home care, so conduct inside a program is squarely covered.
channels.who_to_report: A child under 18 at a Rhode Island program. Every person in Rhode Island is required to report within 24 hours of knowing or suspecting.
channels.how: Call. All calls are recorded, and you may call anonymously.
channels.phone_note: 1-800-RI-CHILD. 24 hours a day, seven days a week.
channels.deadline: The duty is to report within 24 hours of knowing or suspecting - a deadline on the reporter, not on the abuse.

channels.name: Disability Rights Rhode Island
channels.what_it_can_do: Rhode Island's Protection and Advocacy agency, with federal authority to investigate abuse and neglect of people with disabilities in facilities, a right of access to them, and free legal advocacy.
channels.who_to_report: A Rhode Island program where the young person has a disability or a mental health diagnosis.
